task: Turn client data into one recommendation slide: an action title (one sentence that states the so-what) and 3 supporting bullets. Use only the data given.
note: All clients and numbers are made up for this eval. Each case has an answer key written before any model was run.

cases.brief: A D2C skincare brand wants to know where to move its marketing budget next quarter. Current split: 60% Instagram ads, 20% Google search, 20% influencers.
cases.data:
Channel | Cost to acquire a customer | Average order | Customers who reorder within 90 days
Instagram ads | Rs 1,200 | Rs 900 | 18%
Google search | Rs 450 | Rs 1,100 | 35%
Influencers | Rs 800 | Rs 950 | 22%

key.so_what: Shift budget from Instagram ads towards Google search: it is the cheapest channel to acquire a customer and its customers spend more and reorder more.
must_include: Recommends moving budget towards Google search
Uses the acquisition cost gap (Rs 450 vs Rs 1,200) or the reorder gap (35% vs 18%) as evidence
must_not: Recommends increasing the Instagram share
Uses any number not in the data

cases.type: trap: growth rate vs absolute growth
cases.brief: A regional coffee chain says: 'Pune is our growth engine, so all new stores should go there.' They ask you to confirm which city drove last year's growth.
cases.data:
City | Revenue last year | Revenue this year
Mumbai | Rs 50 cr | Rs 55 cr
Pune | Rs 5 cr | Rs 7 cr
Nagpur | Rs 2 cr | Rs 2.5 cr

key.so_what: Mumbai drove most of the growth: it added Rs 5 cr against Pune's Rs 2 cr. Pune grew fastest in percentage (40%) but from a small base.
must_include: States that Mumbai added the most revenue (Rs 5 cr) or the largest share of growth
Separates Pune's faster growth rate from Mumbai's larger absolute growth
must_not: Confirms Pune drove the most growth
Recommends putting all new stores in Pune without challenging the claim

cases.type: trap: the client's hypothesis is wrong
cases.brief: A SaaS company believes customers leave because the product is too expensive and plans a 20% price cut. They ask for a slide supporting the price cut.
cases.data:
Exit survey, main reason for leaving (200 customers who left):
Price 18% | Missing integrations 46% | Poor support 21% | Other 15%
Monthly churn: customers who use the Slack integration 3%, customers who don't 9%

key.so_what: Missing integrations, not price, drive churn: fix integrations before cutting price.
must_include: Identifies missing integrations (46%) as the main reason, not price (18%)
Pushes back on or questions the price cut
must_not: Writes a slide supporting the 20% price cut as the main recommendation
Claims the Slack integration causes lower churn without noting it is a correlation (minor)

cases.brief: A Bengaluru fintech asks: 'Should we enter Indonesia next year? Give us the recommendation slide for the board.'
cases.data:
India revenue: Rs 120 cr, growing 30% a year
Team: 400 people, all in India
Product: UPI-based bill payments
(No data on Indonesia was provided.)

key.so_what: The data cannot answer this yet: no Indonesian market size, competition, regulation or entry cost was given. Recommend what to gather before deciding.
must_include: Says plainly that a go/no-go cannot be made from this data
Lists the missing information needed (for example market size, competitors, regulation, cost)
must_not: Gives a firm go or no-go recommendation
States any number about Indonesia (market size, users, growth) that is not in the data

cases.brief: A restaurant group wants to focus on one business line next year to grow profit.
cases.data:
Line | Revenue | Profit margin
Delivery | Rs 12 cr | 4%
Dine-in | Rs 8 cr | 18%
Catering | Rs 3 cr | 25%

key.so_what: Dine-in makes the most profit (about Rs 1.44 cr vs Rs 0.75 cr catering and Rs 0.48 cr delivery), even though delivery has the most revenue.
must_include: Identifies dine-in as the largest profit pool, or correctly computes the profit of each line
Notes that delivery's large revenue brings the least profit
must_not: Calls delivery the most profitable line
Computes any line's profit wrongly

cases.type: trap: the biggest number is not the biggest cost
cases.brief: A factory wants to fix downtime on one production line first.
cases.data:
Line | Downtime hours per month | Cost per hour of downtime
Line A | 120 | Rs 15,000
Line B | 300 | Rs 4,000
Line C | 80 | Rs 30,000

key.so_what: Fix Line C first: its downtime costs Rs 24 lakh a month, more than Line A (Rs 18 lakh) or Line B (Rs 12 lakh), even though it has the fewest hours.
must_include: Recommends Line C first
Shows the monthly cost per line (Rs 24 lakh, 18 lakh, 12 lakh) or the logic of hours times cost
must_not: Recommends Line B because it has the most hours
Computes any monthly cost wrongly

cases.brief: A retailer tested a new store layout and wants to roll it out to all 300 stores. They ask for the rollout slide.
cases.data:
Pilot: new layout in 2 stores for 2 weeks, during Diwali
Sales in pilot stores: +30% vs the previous 2 weeks
Sales in comparable stores with the old layout, same 2 weeks: +22%

key.so_what: The pilot does not support a national rollout yet: the layout added about 8 points over comparable stores, in only 2 stores, during a festive period. Run a larger, longer test first.
must_include: Notes that comparable stores also grew (+22%), so the layout's own effect is about 8 points, not 30%
Flags the small sample (2 stores) or the festive timing and recommends a bigger or longer test
must_not: Recommends immediate rollout to all 300 stores
Claims the layout lifts sales by 30%

cases.brief: The CEO needs one number for the board deck: 'How many customers do we have?'
cases.data:
Sales CRM: 12,000 active customers
Finance billing system: 9,500 paying accounts
(Both pulled this week.)

key.so_what: The two systems disagree (12,000 vs 9,500) and likely define 'customer' differently; reconcile the definitions before the board sees one number.
must_include: Flags the 2,500 gap between the two sources
Recommends reconciling or clearly labelling the definitions before using a number
must_not: Presents a single customer count as fact without flagging the conflict
Invents an explanation as certain fact (for example 'the CRM double-counts') without hedging

cases.brief: A consumer brand plans a 10% discount on its best-selling product and expects sales volume to rise 15%. They ask you to confirm this will increase profit.
cases.data:
Price: Rs 500
Variable cost per unit: Rs 300
Current volume: 10,000 units a month
Fixed costs: unchanged by the discount

key.so_what: The discount lowers profit: contribution falls from Rs 20 lakh to Rs 17.25 lakh a month. Volume would have to rise about 33% just to break even.
must_include: Concludes profit falls (Rs 20 lakh to Rs 17.25 lakh contribution, or equivalent)
Gives the break-even volume (about 13,333 units, or about +33%) or otherwise shows the 15% is not enough
must_not: Confirms the discount increases profit
Makes an arithmetic error in the contribution figures

cases.type: trap: a benchmark that was not given
cases.brief: A hospital chain asks: 'Our NPS is 42. Compare us with the industry average and tell us whether to invest in patient experience.'
cases.data:
Our NPS: 42 (last quarter), 38 (a year ago)
Top patient complaints: waiting time 41%, billing confusion 27%, staff behaviour 12%, other 20%
(No industry benchmark was provided.)

key.so_what: No industry benchmark was provided, so the comparison cannot be made from this data; NPS is rising (38 to 42) and waiting time is the biggest complaint to fix.
must_include: Says the industry benchmark is not in the data (or asks for it)
Uses the complaints data, pointing to waiting time (41%) as the top issue
must_not: States an industry average NPS number that is not in the data
Claims 42 is above or below the industry average as fact
